content: IN your Life of the Right Reverend Bishop Bull, the principal, and indeed the Only Considerable Objection you allege against my Book, is; that almost all my Citations out of that Learned Author are represented in a very different View from That which the Author had certainly in writing those Passages; as are also the Citations out of the Fathers themselves, which Dr. Clarke here met with, and both accommodated to his own purpose, and That frequently without so much as the least Notice taken of the Explications and Answers given to them by Bishop Bull. This Objection, you are sensible, I had indeavoured to prevent; by declaring beforehand, that I cited Modern Authors and Fathers too, not with any intention to show what was in the whole the Opinion of those Authors; (for the Question was to be determined by Scripture only, and not by Human Authority;) but I cited them, only to show what Important Concessions they were obliged to make; even such Concessions, as of Necessity and in strictness

label: paragraph_title

label: text

ness of Argument inferred my Conclusion, whether the Authors themselves made any such Inference or no. And This you do indeed very justly and fairly acknowledge. But still, notwithstanding this reasonable Acknowledgment, you continue to allege, that it is enough to have shewn what manner of Judgement we ought to make of Dr Clarke's Citations, for they are generally applied much after the same Manner and with the same Views; and you call it (in a less kind manner than usual,) the Doctors Artful Way of citing Authors and Books, and infinate that therefore my Quotations are not much to be depended upon. That sometimes they are not indeed much to be depended upon, for knowing (as you say) the Opinion or Judgment of any Writer; is very true, because they were not brought for That Purpose: But then they are very much to be depended upon for another and far more material reason, viz. for knowing the Truth itself of Things. And in order to This End, they are always so much the more to be depended upon, and the more to be regarded; as the Author, from whom they are cited, was upon the whole more different in his Opinion, from what those particular Citations seem to express. For Writers upon controversial Points, feldom make more Concessions in favour of any opinion different from their own, than the Weight of Truth and

A 3 Reason

label: paragraph_title

label: text
content: Reason necessarily extorts from them. Wherefore in citing and making Use of such Concessions, there is no other Artfulness, than that most justifiable one of drawing Arguments strong and conclusive from such Premises, as even an Adversary is of necessity forced to grant. Nor needs it at all to be regarded, that some of the Writers, from whom such Citations are taken, do themselves indeavour sometimes to draw Conclusions very different. For in all Argumentation whatsoever, it is well known that the Premises only are of any Weight; and that Conclusions always stand for nothing, except the Reader finds himself compelled to draw them, as well as the Writer. Nevertheless, though the Truth of the Scripture-Doctrine does not at all depend upon it, yet, for the satisfaction of such as are apt to pay a greater deference to Authority than is reasonable, I shall not omit taking this occasion to assure you, that, as far as I am able to judge from the whole Course and Tenour of the Writings of the Antients, All the passages cited in my whole Book from the following Principal Writers, viz. Clemens Romanus, Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Origen, Novatian and Eusebius, are not only particular Concessions, but do express what seems moreover to have been in the whole the real Sentiments of the respective Writers themselves: And in the First Part

It is a large Chapter; and the Design of it throughout, is to explain how Christ is truly God and Lord, and yet that at the same time the Father is strictly and emphatically the One and Only God. The whole Chapter is worth every learned persons perusal: But the Sum of it, is This. When the Scripture speaks of False Gods, it always does it, says he [cum aliquo additamento & significatione, per quam ostenduntur non esse dii,] with the Addition of some word which shows them to be indeed No Gods; as when it calls them the Gods of the Gentiles, or the like: But whenever it uses the word [God or Lord] absolutely, and without any such additional explication; then (says he) it always means a person who is truly and really God or Lord; That is to say, either God the Father [qui dominatur omnium] who ruleth over All, or the Son [qui dominium ACCEPIT a Patre suo omnis conditionis] who RECIEVED from his Father dominion over the whole Creation: According

Now in every part of this Reasoning of yours, there is (I think) something defective. For how many Other Attributes and Perfections soever, Origen in his Book ascribes to the Son; yet unless he ascribed Supremacy also, (which he no where does, but on the contrary every where expressly and with great caution excludes it,) this cannot at all affect the Question: See my Scripture-doctrine, pag. 359 and 266. And though he had indeed in Other clear and undoubted passages (which yet he no where has) asserted the Son to be Supreme as well as the Father; yet it would not at all follow (unless Origen were a Writer infallibly consistent with himself,) that he did not interpret the particular text referred to, in the manner that I affirmed him to interpret it. And though Bp. Bull does indeed indeavour to show, that Origen in the place here referred to, speaks of Christ as an Exemplar in his humane Nature; yet he expressly acknowledges [si daremus Origenem ibi loqui de Christo quatenus Deus est,—baud minus recte ea ratione Patri primas tribuere potuit,] that if it be granted that Origen there speaks concerning Christ as God, yet—as deriving—from the Fountain of the Father, he might rightly.

label: text
content: rightly, even in this sense, yield the prebeminence to the Father: Which acknowledgment is all that I cited him for; and therefore it ought not to be suggested that I had cited him unfairly. As to the distinction you allege, that here is not the least Word said, that can justly be interpreted of the Son's Inferiority to the Father in NATURE, but rather the contrary: I shall not contend with you about metaphysical Words, which since I have constantly avoided because of their Abstract and Ambiguous Signification, you should not have chosen to use them in representing my Sense. Bishop Bull expressly owns the Person of the Son to be, in his Highest Capacity, subordinate to the Person of the Father: Which is a Notion very intelligible, (whatever be the Nature, Substance or Essence of either;) and is all (I think) that the Honour of God and the Whole Doctrine of Scripture obliges us to contend for. The Word, Nature, (as it signifies the Nature of any Person, abstract from the Person himself,) is a Metaphysical Term, of great Ambiguity and Obscureness, and of no Use that I know of in any Question, but to introduce more Difficulties by dark Expressions, than are really found in the Things themselves.

Mr Bull first proveth &c. — And there is nothing in this whole Method, nor in any particular Argument under it, which doth tend in the least to favour such an Inequality of NATURE in Father and Son, as is included in That Scheme which it is brought to support. The passage here referred to, are those words of the learned Bp. Bull, wherein he declares and approves the opinion of the Antient Fathers, that the Angel of the Lord (Acts 7, 30,) which appeared to Moses in the Bush, and said, I am the God of thy Fathers, was the Son appearing in his Fathers Name. Now since the Scripture every where represents the Father, as absolutely Invisible; and those Antient Writers, whose Opinions Bp Bull cites and approves, always suppose it impious to imagine that the Supreme God and Father of All ever appeared visibly in his own Person; the Inference I designed should be drawn from hence, is, that the Person of the Son is Subordinate to the Person of the Father, whose Angel or Messenger he is, and in whose Name and by whose Mission he appears. All this, the learned Bp. makes no scruple to grant; and therefore 'twas no misrepresentation of his words, to cite them

label: text
content: But the Observation is not so soon put an End to, as He conceives: For, his Conclusion runs much faster than his Premises. And were it ever so true, that the word $[\tilde{\epsilon}_{is}]$ could justly be rendred, One Being; it would still amount to the same thing: For One Being, when spoken of an Intelligent Agent, is the very same as One Person; Neither is there in Nature any other Notion of a Person, than as it signifies an Intelligent Agent or Intelligent Being: Whenever the word is used otherwise, no Man can tell what it signifies: And of What Use are words, when they have no Signification? Could therefore the word $[\tilde{\epsilon}_{is}]$ possibly have been rendred, as your Friend would have it, One Being; it would have availed him nothing, against any thing I had affirmed. But that it cannot possibly be so rendred, I still affirm; and I am willing to put it upon This short and plain issue: If there be Any One Passage in Any One Greek or Latin Writer in

label: header

content: in the World, accurate or inaccurate, wherein the word [ἐς, Unus] or any other masculine Adjective, placed absolutely without any antecedent Substantive, (as ἐδὲς and ἐς are placed in this Text,) can possibly signify either Thing or Being, or anything else besides Person; I will acknowledge my Explication of This Text to be erroneous. Your Friend might as well have affirmed that, in English, the word, Man, signifies a House or a Ship; or that any other word signifies any other thing whatsoever; as that the word, [ἐς, Unus] can signify Thing or Being. 'Tis certain that Arguments run very low indeed, when all Grammar is forced to be reversed in such a manner, as would make every Language a mere Babel of words, without Any determinate Signification. By Grammar, I mean, not only the artificial Rules of Grammarians, but the common and natural Sense of Mankind. As, when in English we use the word, He; 'tis impossible to mean thereby a Thing or a Being in general, but only an Intelligent Agent or Being, that is, a Person. Thus likewise in Greek, ὀν ὑντες, can signify nothing but Persons; παν ὑντας, nothing but Things. When the Platonists speak of God, considered merely as the Self-existent Being, abstract from the consideration of Life, Action and Government; they then call him ὂν, The Being: But when

label: text
content: But the word [ἐς] One, may in this Text (he says) be Masculine, by reason of its relation to God, [ὁεῖς.] I answer; This cannot possibly be, because Then (the same being to be said of ἐς also,) the full construction would be, There is None Good, [὇δεις αγαθός, there is no God Good,] but One God, that is God: Whereas the plain construction is, There is no Person Good, but One Person, which is God. Had our Saviour meant to say, (as he might, very properly,) There is no Being Good, but One, that is, God; (which yet would not have denoted That sort of Goodness which is Moral, but that which is Natural or Metaphysical;) he must have expressed it thus, ἐδεν αγαθόν, εἰ μη εν, οὐ θεὸς: in like manner as the Philosopher says, ἐδεν γολαςιπυς, εἰ μη εν, οὐ ανρρωπος, [Nibil risibile est, nift Unum, nempe Homo;] Nothing is capable of Laughter, but only One thing, namely Man, or, the Species of Mankind. Had he said, ἐδειες γολαςιπυς εἰ μη εν, οὐ ανρρωπιο, [Nemo risibilis, nift Unus, nempe Homo;] No One [that is, No Person] is capable of Laughter, but One, namely Man, or Mankind; the Expression had been manifestly absurd:

label: header

content: abfurd: Which shows that these Two manners of Expression cannot possibly be confounded. And though Two different Sentences, may sometimes by Accident be nearly of the same import; (as, There is No Being Good, but One, that is God; or, There is No Person Good, but One, that is God;) yet the same Words that express One of these Sentences, cannot possibly express the Other.

label: text
content: Yes; the word [εις, Unus, One,] is no less fitted (he says) to represent Being, than Person; because Neither of them are Masculine. But This is a great mistake: For the word, Person, is always express both in Greek and Latin by the Masculine Adjective, and by It Only; there being no other word either in Greek or Latin, by which it ever was or can possibly be express. Persona, and დენისთი, and მორჩალი, are all of them words of a quite different Sense, and never used by any good Author (unless in very figurative Constructions) in this Signification. I answer: Literally speaking, the whole Number of Christ's Disciples can no more properly be called One Thing, than One Person; and figuratively speaking, they may as well be called One Person, as One Thing. And that St Paul does in this place intend to call the Church, in such a figurative manner of speaking, One Person; (besides that the word, ἐς, necessarily so signifies,) will appear from the following considerations. In the whole New Testament it is very usual to compare the Christian Church to a Body, whereof Christ is the Head; and particular Christians (faith the Apostle) are Members of his Body, of his Flesh, and of his Bones, Eph. 5, 30. In puruance of which elegant Similitude, the Church is often represented under the Notion of a Person, under the Character of the Spouse of Christ: 2 Cor. 11, 2, I have espoused you to one Husband, that I may present you a chaste Virgin [ὑμῶς παρὰν αγυπτ] to Christ: And Rev. 21, 9; 19, 7, I will show thee the Bride, the Lambs Wife;—The marriage of the Lamb is come, and his Wife has made herself ready; and to Her was granted, that she should be arrayed in fine Linen, clean and white; for the fine Linen is the Righteousness of Saints. Thus likewise in the passage before us, Gal. 3, 27, Ye have put on Christ; There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither Bond nor Free, there is neither Male nor Female; for ye are all [ἐς,] considered as One Person in Christ Jesus. Your learned Friend did not at all perceive the Elegancy and Beauty of the Apostle's Expression in this Place. Consider the Church as One Thing, as a Congregation or Body of Men, and all these natural Relations still continue distinct; But consider it under the Notion of one Person, the Spouse of Christ, and then all these differences and distinctions vanish. By the same Figure of Speech, the Jewish Church is stiled in Scripture the Daughter of Sion: Nations and Empires are, in the Prophecy of Daniel, personated as Kings: The Church in the Revelation, under Persecution, is a Woman flying into the Wilderness: The False Church abusing the temporal Power of Princes, to persecute good Christians; is the Woman, the Whore, riding upon a Scarlet-coloured (or bloody) Beast. Deceivers and False-Teachers, are the False-Prophet, Rev. 19, 20, The Beast—and the False-Prophet were cast alive into a Lake of Fire: The Body of corrupt Christians in the latter Ages of the World, are The Man of Sin, 2 Th. 2, 3; and Anti-Christ; 2 Joh. 7, Many Deceivers are entred into the World.

Be it so: The Question then remains, Who That God is, of whom this is spoken. The Jews to be sure, when these words were spoken by Moses, could understand them of no other than of the Almighty Father, the Creator and Governor of all things: And the natural Apprehension, or common Sense of Mankind, obviously leads all Men to understand them after the same manner. content: Now to these Reasons, I reply :

label: text
content: 1. To deny that the Term, Only, always excludes every thing else, but the Subject it is applied to; is to deny that Words have any Signification. For if the word, Only or Alone, does not appropriate; there is no word in any Language, which can appropriate any thing to any Subject.

content: God the Father, because it is itself nothing but an Attribute of God the Father; and to say that the Wisdom of God does any thing, is only saying in other words that God does it himself. But affirming any thing to belong to One Person Alone, is of necessity denying that same thing to belong to any Other Person in the same sense. Whatever therefore is appropriated to the Father alone, is of necessity denied to belong to the Son in that same sense, in which it is appropriated to the Father. Unless it be declared (according to the Sabellian Notion, which upon the Whole amounts to the very same with Socinianism;) that the Son is not a real Person, but a mere Attribute of the Father. Which Opinion your Friend disclaims, though his Reasoning here necessarily supposes it.

I made no Use of that critical Remark, in My Book; and yet your learned Friend is very unfortunate, in asserting that That Remark is evidently false. label: text
content: These words are so express and full a declaration of God the Father's being by way of Eminence the One God, that there are no possible words by which it could have been afferted more explicitly. Had the

label: text
content: the Apostle said only, To Us there is but One God, and one Lord Jesus Christ; there had really, according to the Analogy of Scripture, been no Ambiguity: But when he adds by way of Interpretation, as it were on purpose to prevent all possibility of mistake, there is but One God, the FATHER; and one Lord, Jesus Christ; it is a very furprizing thing, to find a Learned and Sincere Man indeavouring to put another Sense upon the words, One God; different from That which the Apostle in such express words declares himself to mean.

label: text
content: But (fays your learned Friend) it is plain here, that the Unity of God is affirmed in opposition to Idols. Very true: But it is plain also, that the God, whose Unity is here so affirmed, is by the Apostle expressly declared to be the Father.

label: text

That the Father's being by way of Eminence the One God, does not exclude the Son from being truly God by true communication of Divinity from that one unoriginated God the Father, I readily acknowledge. But to say that the One God the Father is the Son also, and not the Father only; or that the Son is not excluded from E 3 being

label: text

I answer: Not only God the Father, but God the Father and Son and Holy Ghost, must needs by your Friend be allowed to be Pure Deity: And consequently, if the Apostle had here mentioned Jesus Christ in the second place (as your Friend supposes) only upon Account of his being (as God-man) a Being distinct from pure Deity; he must have said, not, One God, the Father; but One God, the Father and Son and Holy Ghost; and one Lord (or God-man) Jesus Christ. content: understood this Text in any other Sense. Why then does he seek for a New Interpretation, unsupported either by Scripture or Antiquity? If the Term God, says he, can be applied to the Holy Ghost, [for Proof whereof he refers to five Texts, in not one of which the Term is so applied;] why should there be so much pains taken to prove it to belong to the Father, who is not mentioned in the Context? I answer: It requires no great Pains or Force, to understand the word, God, in this Text, as signifying the Father; because in All other Texts the same word always signifies the Father, and in No other Text ever signifies the Holy Ghost. The word occurs in the New Testament above One Thousand times, and in all those passages, (excepting three or four in which it is applied to the Son,) it always signifies the Father, (as I have shown demonstratively in my Scripture-doctrine,) and is in no place applied to the Holy Ghost. In what Sense, and with what Propriety of Speech, the Holy Spirit may, or may not, be stiled God, (which your Friend indeavours to intermix in his Argument,) is not here the Question: but whether in fact he is, or is not, so stiled in This or in any other Text of Scripture. The Holy Ghost, is the Holy Spirit of God; that is to say, the Holy Spirit of the Father: And if the word, God, placed abso-

The only Argument your Friend urges, why the word, God, in this Text, should be meant of the Holy Ghost, and not of the Father; is This very obscure one: That if the word God here signified the Father, then it would follow that the Holy Ghost acted by the Authority of the Father; which since the Apostles themselves also did, it would follow that They might have been stiled the Objects of the Lie, as well as the Holy Ghost; the Person of the Spirit being as little affected with the Lie spoken, in comparison of the Authority affronted in Him, as the Persons of the Apostles were affected by it in comparison of the Authority affronted in Them; Neither could a Lie against the Holy Ghost, have been said comparatively to be none against Men, if the Holy Ghost were not He who is here stiled God. I am sure I have represented his Argument more clear and strong, than the Author himself represented it; and yet at the best it is a very obscure one. The Strength of it indeed, is no more than this: If the Holy Ghost be at all subordinate to the Father, (as the Scripture every where declares he is sent and given by Him.)

label: text

label: text

label: text
content: Of the latter of these Expositions, your Learned Friend takes not the least Notice. I suppose, he overlooked it, as not being in its proper place, but in the Addenda, pag. 1; Though he elsewhere takes Notice of something else mentioned in That Page.

label: text
content: Now that the Word [φινος] in Scripture, does not signify the Nature of things in the metaphysical or essential, but only in the vulgar and natural, the moral or political Sense of the Word; that is, the true State and Condition of things, their Capacities and Powers, their Circumstances and Qualifications, the Reason of things, and sometimes even Customs only; appears from the Use of the same Word, 1 Cor. 11, 14, Doth not even Nature itself teach you, that if a Man bath long Hair, it is a shame unto him? & Rom. 2, 14, do by Nature the things contained

And thus likewise in the present Passage; Them which by their Nature, (that is, which in the Nature and Reason and Truth of Things,) are no Gods; have no divine, no invisible Authority or Dominion over you; have nothing of That Nature, which you vainly ascribe to them; nothing of That Dominion and Power, which the Worship you pay them supposes them to have. And This is the True Notion of Idolatry: viz. the ascribing to any Being, real or imaginary, such invisible Dominion or Power, and consequently such Worship and Honour, as does not belong to it. label: text
content: As to the Text itself, the True Meaning of it seems to Me to be this: That in the like Sense as God the Father is in other places of Scripture declared to be the One and Only God, he is in this place declared to be also the One and Only Good. That is to say: As God the Father is, by way of Eminence, the One and Only God, because He Alone has [ἀντοθεόπτα] Divinity absolutely of Himself, Supreme, Unoriginate, and not derived from Any; (as Origen learnedly and at large argues in the place before-cited; See above, pag. 65.) and yet Christ is also True God, because he has True Divinity derived to him from the Father; whereas all False Gods, are no Gods at all: So God the Father is likewise, by way of Eminence, the One and Only Good, because He Alone is [ἀντομαγὴν] the original underived Fountain of Goodness; and yet Christ also is Truly Good, by having the Father's Goodness communicated to him without Measure; whereas False Gods, have neither Any Dominion, nor Any Goodness at all.

label: text
content: I reply: His affirming Self-originated and Begotten, to be, not essential, but personal Characters; is affirming, in other Words, that they are, not essential, but essential Characters. For What is a personal Character, but a Character which distinguishes That particular Person from all other Persons? and What is This, but the Essence of That Person? If we know any thing of the Essence of God, the first and of all others the most essential Character of him, is his being Self-existent or Unoriginated. The Substance of the Son, whatever the Nature of it be in other respects, yet is certainly derived from the Father; otherwise, the Son being Self-existent as well as the Father, it would follow, that Not the Person of the Son, (that is, Not the Son himself,) but the Personality only of the Son was begotten of the Father: Which is unintelligible Metaphysicks, and without any Foundation in Scripture. However, your Friend, by allowing the Son to be Begotten, and the Father alone to be Self-originated or (to speak more properly) Unoriginated; clearly grants All that I contend for: Though, at the same time, by darkning it

label: text
content: I observe one thing further upon This Head. Your Friend is very fond of confounding All Language. In the first Text he quotes, he will have [εις] to signify One Thing, instead of One Person. And here he would have [εις ἀστὴν] to signify, in Him, instead of, to Him: The Particle, he says, being Frequently so used. But there is no such thing in the World, as putting one Word, in this manner, for another: And indeed it is impossible there should; For, at that rate, no Language would have any Signification. Some Grammarians indeed give Instances of one Word's seeming to be put for another; But the Instances they allege, are always either Corruptions of the Copies, or else their own Mistakes. There are some places in the New Testament, where our Translators render [εις ἀστὴν] in him; But where-ever they do so, 'tis because they mistake the Sense. Thus 1 Cor. 8, 6, To us there is but One God, the Father; of whom are all things, and We In him: In the Greek it is [εις ἀστὴν] and we To him: That is, To or For his Glory; Or, (as the Learned Mr Mede paraphrases it,) to whom as Supreme we are

The like vulgar Error, with regard to the Particle [in] in the Latin Language, I have refuted in my Annotations upon Cafars Commentaries, ad lib. 4. de Bello Gallico, pag. 76, lin. 12. Sometimes indeed one and the same Word has indifferently two or more significations; and then it may (according as the Sense requires) be understood in Any of those Significations. Thus the Word [ἐπὶ] in the New Testament, according to the Genius of the Hebrew and Hellenistical Stile, signifies indifferently In or By. But there is no such thing in any Language, as putting one Word for another; And therefore εἰς ἀντον, (the Word εἰς having but one signification,) can be rendred no otherwise than To Him.

The Design of the Apostle is not to prove (as your Friend supposes,) that we Are in Christ; but to infer from thence, (That being the Premise, not the Conclusion of his Argument,) that in like manner as Those who are in the World, (ver. 19,) are thereby [ἐν τὴν ποντηρ] in the Evil One, and, because they have not the Son, therefore neither have they the Father, ch. 2, 23; so We, on the contrary, who Are in Christ, are

For whatever is caused by an Intelligent Being, is caused by the Will of That Being. Otherwise it is not (in Truth and Reality) caused by That Being at all, but by some Superior Cause, (be it Necessity, or Fate, or Whatever it be;) under which, the Intelligent Being is in such Case as much an Instrument only, as if it was wholly Unintelligent. For which Reason, All the Learnedest of the Orthodox Fathers, who understood how to argue closely and strongly; Justin Martyr, Origen, Novatian, Eusebius, the Council of Sirmium, Marius Victorinus, Basil, Gregory Nyssen, and indeed almost all Antient Writers excepting only Athanasius; professedly argue (as I have shown at large in my Scripture-doctrine, Part II, §. 17,) that the Son was generated of the Father, not by absolute Necessity of Nature, but by an Act of his eternal Power and Will. label: text
content: The Title, Lord God, in the common and natural Apprehension of all Mankind, and in the constant Usage of Scripture, is a PERSONAL Character; expressing, not speculative and metaphysical Qualities, but Personal and Relative Perfections, namely Dominion and Government over the World. As appears plainly from the Relative Terms so frequently joined with it, OUR God, OUR Lord God, the God OF HEAVEN, and the like: None of which Terms can be joined with metaphysical Appellations, which are Absolute and not Relative; such as are, The Infinite Being, The Eternal Being, and the like.

label: text
content: By this Term therefore, Lord God, in the present Text, must of necessity be meant either God the Father, considered as Supreme and absolute Lord of all; or else the Son, who, by communication of the Father's Power and Dominion, is also, in Subordination to Him, truly Lord of all.

label: text
content: In which foever of these Senses it be underfstood, nothing can from this Text be H 4 inferred

label: header
content: A Commentary

label: text
content: inferred contrary to any thing I have affirmed. For if the Title, Lord God, be here applied to the Son; it is still applied to him in the Sense now explained: And if it be meant of the Father, (as I think is more probable;) then the latter part of the Text is, by an easy Figure, a Transition from the Person of Him who is the Invisible God, to the Person of Him who is the Image of the Invisible God, and who always acts and speaks in His Name and Authority. A Figure not unusual, either in Scripture or other Authors. See my Scripture-doctrine, No 538, 597, 616 & 1056: Also 1 Job. 3, 1, compared with ver. 5.

label: text
content: Your Friend contends that the Title, Lord God, is here given to the Son. And if it was so, in the Sense wherein his own Quotations out of the Fathers (as I shall show presently) give that Title to Christ; it would not prove any thing at all against Me. For Most of those Fathers, in those very Passages he cites, explain themselves (as will appear immediately) in the very same manner as I have done. But your Friend, not content to understand these words in the Text, in the same Sense as the like words are found in his Quotations; labours to suggest another Sense, which yet he cares not to express distinctly, but leaves it darkly to his Reader to infer as well as he can. If his words infer any thing; it must

label: paragraph_title
content: on Luke 1; 16, 17.

label: text
content: must be, that the Son is so stiled Lord God, as not to be distinguished from the Father: Which, when expressed intelligibly, can end in nothing else, (though your Friend seems not to intend it.) but in denying the Son to have Any Being at all: Which is the Socinian Notion. And What Need is there of interpreting Scripture after so unintelligible a manner, when All the Texts in their obvious and natural Sense carry with them another Signification? That which seems to have led your Friend into This, is a Notion he has entertained of certain Scripture-Interpretations justly Conceived to be founded upon TRADITION, and of certain Doctrines and Expositions of the Sacred Writings, handed down to the Fathers by TRADITION from Their Fathers. What and where this Tradition is, it does not appear: For the Greater Part of the Fathers plainly enough expresses the very Notion I am pleading for; (as the Reader will see presently in those very Passages, which your Friend has cited to prove the contrary:) But What that Doctrine is, which your Friend alludes to as Traditionary, remains very obscure; and he himself leaves it to his Reader to guess at, rather than any where explicitly expresses it. What he drops in different places, amounts (if any thing) to a Total Confusion of Persons: Which Persons he sometimes speaks of.

content: of, as being One subordinate to Another ; and at other times, as if he thought them All but One Person. Your Friend being a sincere and sober-minded Man, has entred only a little way into these Traditionary Explications of Scripture : But those who have gone far into them, (as some late Writers have done,) have given such Vifionary and Cakbalistical Interpretations, especially of the Old Testament; as give too sad an Occasion for Infidels to look upon all Religion as Enthusiasm; and particularly have caused the Study of the Hebrew Language, (which in itself is a plain, easy, inartificial Language,) to be brought (by Men of weak Judgments abusing it) into the utmost Contempt.

label: text
content: But to proceed to particulars.

label: text
content: It seems to Me that the Term, Lord God, in the Text before us, signifies the Father. My Reason is, because this Title, the Lord God, when used absolutely, and without any antecedent Mention of the Person it refers to, does in Scripture-Language, by way of Eminence, Always signify the Father. Thus in this very Chapter, Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, (says Zacharias, ver. 68,) for that he hath raised up an horn of Salvation for us in the House of his Servant David; viz. for that he hath raised up unto us That Lord, before whom John the Baptist was to go, ver. 76. To This,

label: header
content: on Luke 1; 16, 17.

label: text
content: This, your Friend replies, that elsewhere $^S$ Thomas calls Christ, My Lord and my God. But I answer, This is plainly meant in That Sense, in which $^S$ Paul applies to him the Title God in that Citation out of the Psalmist; Thy Throne, O God, is for ever and ever; thou hast loved Righteousness; therefore GOD, even THY GOD, [or, therefore, O God, THY GOD] hath anointed thee, &c. Your Friend alleges but one Text more, Rev. 22, 6, The Lord God of the Holy Prophets sent his Angel: And this he thinks is meant of the Son, because it is said, Rev. 1, 1, that Jesus sent his Angel. As if it might not very properly be said, that God the Father sent That Angel, whom Christ sent forth with that Revelation which God the Father gave him to send by the Angel. There are in Scripture innumerable Instances of the like manner of speaking. And that the Lord God of the Holy Prophets does indeed here signify the Father, is evident from hence, that, in the five fore-going Verses of the same Chapter, the word, God, and Lord God, are used two or three times in express contradiction to the Lamb.

label: text
content: As to the Passages your Friend cites out of the Old Testament; if they be understood literally, (in the manner he cites and applies them,) they prove too much for him, viz. that Christ is God the Father himself;

But if they must not be thus understood, (as he will grant they must not, though he takes no Care to avoid it;) then they can no otherwise be understood, than according to St Stephen's Explication, Acts 7, 30, where he says, The Angel of the Lord appeared to Moses in a Flame of Fire in the Bush. Saying, I am the God of thy Fathers; Which is plainly the Angel of God's presence speaking in the Name and Person and Authority of the Father.

label: text
content: And in This Sense, if the Title, Lord God, in the Text before us, be understood of the Son, it will not prove any thing against Me. Any more than your Friend's Citations out of the Fathers do: Which when the Reader compares, he will be surprised to find almost all of them most fully and plainly expressing that Sense I am now speaking of, and not at all That which your Friend cites them for.

label: text
content: JOHN I, 1. And the Word was God.

label: text
content: Of these words, I said, there are only Three Possible Interpretations. The first is that the word was That same Person, whom he was with: And This is both a Contradiction in Terms, and also the antient Heresy of Sabellius. The second is; that the Word was Another Self-existent, Underived, Independent Person, co-ordinate to Him with whom he was: And This is the Impiety of Polytheism; subverting that First and Great Foundation of All Religion both Natural and Revealed, the Unity of GOD. The third is; that the Word is a Person, (not λόγος συνδιαθετος the internal Reason or Wisdom of God, which is merely an Attribute of the Father; but a Person, whose Name is called The Word of God, Rev. 19, 13: The Interpreter and Messenger of his Father, λόγος — τὸ ἐπιστὰ πάλειος ἔφυμενεύς "Αγγελῶν, Athanasf. contra Gentes: God by communication of Divinity from Him who is of Himself God, μετοχή τὴν 'Auθοδὲ θυσποίη-

label: paragraph_title

label: text
content: mer, Origen. in Job. pag. 46:) a Person, deriving from the Father (with whom he existed before the World was,) both his Being itself, and incomprehensible Power and Knowledge, and other divine Attributes and Authority, in a Manner not revealed, and which Humane Wifdom ought not to presume to be able more particularly to explain.

label: text
content: Against this Exposition of mine, your Friend alleges nothing but a metaphysical Inquiry, concerning Substances and Essences ; which the Scripture never at all meddles with, either one way or other : And a figurative Passage out of Clemens Alexandrinus, and another of Irenaus ; which Passages the Reader may understand, by comparing them with other Passages cited above out of the fame Writers.

But if, (which is much more natural, supposing That Reading to be genuine,) it be understood to mean the Father; then either, his own Blood, must signify, the Blood of his own Son; or else the Words, He bath purchased with his own Blood, may still be understood of Christ, in the same manner of speaking that we find used by St Luke, ch. I; 16, 17: Not much unlike to which, is that Transition from one Person to another, which St John uses in his first Epistle, ch. 3, ver. 1, compared with ver. 5.

label: text
content: But your Friend contends for another Interpretation, viz. that the Word, God, signifies in this place Both Father and Son. Of which Confusion, I am very sure there is no Instance in the whole Bible; that one and the same personal and relative Title, such as God or Lord or King or Father or Son or the like; should at one and the same time signify

label: text
content: Two Persons. Yes, he says, St John comprehends the Father and Son under the Name God, in the first verse of his Gospel; and therefore may be supposed to use the

label: header
content: on Acts. 20, 28.

label: text
content: fame Name sometimes for the Father, and sometimes for the Son, or for Both together. But does St John indeed use the Word, God (not only sometimes for the Father, and sometimes for the Son, but also) for Both Together? Verily, had your Friend considered here what he said, I am perswaded he would not have stood to it. For observe what a Paraphrase his Criticism makes, when applied to the Text he directs us to apply it to. John, I, 1. The Word was with God, and the Word was God; that is, The Word was with the Father and the Son, and the Word was the Father and the Son. This is no misrepresentation of his Sense; but is his True, real, and professed Meaning. For his Design is to show, not that the Word, God, means in one part of the Sentence the Son, and in the other the Father; but that the same individual Word singly in one part of the Sentence alone, signifies Both Father and Son. I wonder much, he should not see the Absurdity of it. Well: But in that Passage I referred to, John, 3, 1, he thinks the Case is plain: Behold what manner of Love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the Sons of God: In this place, he says, the Term God may very well be judged to stand for the Father and the Son. Let us see how that can be. Why, the Washing of Regeneration, says he, through the Virtue

label: paragraph_title
content: A Commentary

label: text
content: tue of their Names invoked in Baptism, begets us into Children, so that we are the Sons of Both Persons. By This Argument he should have said, we are the Sons of the Three Persons. But the Scripture gives quite a different Account of this Matter. We are There called The Sons of God, because we are made, in our measure and degree, by Adoption and Grace, what Christ was, in a complete and perfect manner, by Nature: We are represented as Heirs of God, and Joint-Heirs with Christ, that is, Brethren of Christ and Sons of God. If then our being Sons of God, means that we are Sons of the Father and the Son; then also Christ's being the Son of God, means that he is the Son of the Father and the Son. When once Confusion is introduced, there is no End of Absurdities. But your Friend draws one Argument more, from the Word [φανεωρὸν he shall appear,] used in the next verse, 1 John, 3, 2. Now are we the Sons of God, (that is, faith be, of the One God, Father and Son:) But when He shall appear, (that is, faith be, when the One God shall appear in the Person of the Son.) Put now these two Explications together, and then the whole verse stands thus: Now are we the Sons of the Father and the Son; But when the Father and the Son shall appear in the Person of the Son, we shall be like HIM.

label: text
content: These Words, I said, were fully and clearly explained by the parallel Texts, Eph. 3, 9, God created all things By Jesus Christ; and Heb. 1, 2, By whom also He made the Worlds. And in This Explication, all the Antient Fathers, how much soever they differ from each other in Other things, unanimously agree. Even Tertullian, in his Book against Praxeas: [Alium, per quem omnia; alium, a quo omnia:] One, faith he, O F whom are all things; Another, BY (or Through) whom are all things: Commenting this very Text of St John.

label: text

Only, after having expressly granted All that I contend for, viz. that the Son works every thing in Obedience to his Father; the Father working primarily, the Son subordinately: he adds, YET the Son works Freely. For I never thought, (and I believe no body else ever did,) that the Father uses the Son as an Unintelligent, but as an Intelligent Instrument. Whatever the Father does by the Son, he does by the Free Will of the Son, concurring with and accomplishing the good pleasure of his Father. The Son quickneth whom he will, Joh. 5, 21; Freely, and by his own Will: Because, (ver. 22,) the Father hath committed All judgment unto the Son. So again, Job. 10, 18, No Man taketh my Life from me, but I lay it down of myself, [Freely and Willingly:] I have Power to lay it down, and I have Power to take it again; [Because] This Commandment have I received of my Father.

label: text
content: JOHN V, 18. But said also that God was his Father [παιτεία]ov, his own Father,] making himself equal with God.

label: text
content: Your learned Friend, in his Explication of this Text, begins to indulge his Imagination, more than is usual for so calm and reasonable a Writer. The Jews, he says, who drew the Inference, MUST have had

label: header
content: on Joh. 5, 18.

label: text
content: some reason for understanding the Premise in so exalted a Sense, as would infer their Conclusion: that is, they MUST have had a Notion that there was a certain Person so closely united to the Great God——that the Great God was his Proper Father, and that on This account he was Equal with the Father：——For except all this be supposed, it is difficult to account how so extraordinary a Conclusion COULD be drawn from a Premise, that was otherwise capable of a lower Interpretation. Now it is CERTAIN that the Jews, if they understood the Meaning of their own Scriptures, MUST have known, that there was a Divine Person subsisting with the Father——from the Beginning of the World, which is called Wisdom; as is EVIDENT from Prov. 9, 22, The Lord possessed me in the Beginning，and that this Divine Person was brought forth, or begotten, when there were no Depths, Prov. 8, 24; And BY CONSEQUENCE that this Divine Person MUST be the Only begotten。They MUST have also known that God had a Son, Prov. 30, 4; and that This Son is the same with Wisdom or the Only-begotten；otherwise Wisdom could not be the Only begotten, if there be a Son begotten different from Wisdom。The Jews, I say, could not have been ignorant of these great Truths, upon the SUPPOSITION of

label: header
content: A Commentary

label: text
content: their Knowledge of the Scriptures ; and this Knowledge OUGHT to be SUPPOSED, 'till the Contrary be made to APPEAR.

label: text
content: Is not This now a wonderful Flight of Imagination; to conceive that the Affirmative ought always to be Supposed, 'till the Negative appears? that every Man ought to be supposed to know every thing, 'till the contrary appears? and that every Accusation brought against our Saviour by his malitious Enemies, must needs be in Them a True Deduction from True Principles Truly understood? That the Jews, not only understood our Saviours calling God his Father, to be a claiming to himself more than any other Man or Prophet could claim; but that they understood also clearly every thing that was hinted in the Old Testament, even in the obscurest Prophecies, concerning the Greatness and Dignity of his Person? The Apostles, after they had conversed with him for several Years, and, besides their own Knowledge of the Old Testament, had heard Him also frequently explain it to them; and had heard him moreover expressly declare that his Kingdom was not of this World, but that at the End He should come in the Glory of his Father with his Angels to judge the whole World; were yet so ignorant, even after his Resurrection, as to ask him, Lord, wilt thou

label: paragraph_title
content: on John 5,18.

label: text
content: thou at This time restore again the [temporal] Kingdom to Israel : And had the Jews, his Accufers, so perfect a Knowledge of his spiritual Kingdom, as to understand all the literal, and all the mystical Prophecies concerning him, as perfectly as any Christian has ever done to This day? Surely, there never was a more extraordinary Imagination.

label: text
content: The True State of the whole Matter, is plainly no more than This. Our Saviour having healed a Lame Man upon the Sabbath-day, was accused and persecuted by the Jews as a Sabbath-breaker. To This, our Saviour replies, ver. 17, My Father worketh hitherto, and I work: That is to say; Though the works of God are finished from the Foundation of the World, and my Father ceased indeed on the Seventh day from his works of Creation; yet his works of Providence and Goodness go on every day for ever without Intermission; and I likewise do works of Goodness and Charity, even on the Sabbath-day. The Jews, willing to take any handle (though never so unreasonable) of Accusing him, infer, ver. 18, (by way of Calumny, not by way of strict Reasoning,) that his calling God his Father [o πατρὰ μυ] was as much as assuming to Himself, that God who was the common Father of them All, was in a higher and more peculiar manner [πατρὰ ιδιον]

label: paragraph_title
content: A Commentary

label: text
content: His own proper Father: And from This, and from his joyning and comparing his own Works with his Fathers Works in one and the same Sentence, they infer further, in the next step of Calumny, that he made himself equal with God: Meaning thereby, not that he claimed to Himself to be God indeed in Any Sense; (for neither They nor his own Disciples had as yet any the least Thought of That;) but that by Consequence, (which angry Accusers draw very hastily,) he assumed to himself a Power and Authority like That of God. The Expression is the same, and meant in the same Sense, as That other Accusation, Job. 10, 33, Thou, being a Man, makest thy self God: Which was spoken after the same manner, as Men say to an assuming Person, You make your self King; when they intend to charge him with taking upon himself, not the Person, but the State of a Prince. Accordingly, to this Accusation of making himself equal with God, our Saviour replies, ver. 19, not by confounding himself with the Father, (as was to have been expected in your Friend's Scheme,) but by referring all his works To the Father, and showing that he really was (what he pretended to be,) the promised Messiah, the Son of God, sent forth from God, invested with the Power and Authority of the Father: That the Son can do nothing of himself, but what be

label: header
content: on Joh. 5, 18.

label: text
content: he seeth the Father do, ver. 19: That the Father loveth the Son, and showeth him all things that himself doeth, ver. 20: That the Father bath committed all judgment to the Son, ver. 22: That therefore, as all Men honour the Father, so they ought also to honour the Son, to the Honour of the Father which sent him, ver. 23: That, as the Father bath Life in himself, so bath he given to the Son to have Life in himself, ver. 26: That he can of Himself do nothing, and that he seeketh not his own Will, but the Will of the Father which sent him, ver. 30: That the works which he doth, bear witness of him, that the Father bath sent him, ver. 36. This is the Answer he gives to the Jews Accusation; And it shows very plainly what he meant by calling God his Father, (which was the Ground of their Accusation,) and by joining himself with the Father in those words, My Father worketh hitherto, and I work.

label: text
content: But now it is impossible for any Man who reads this very Chapter of Novatian, [cap. 31,] not to see that the words, which your Friend cites, are Corrupt; The express design of the Author in every word of that Chapter, being to show directly on the contrary, that, if they were absolutely Equal, then and for that very reason they would of necessity be Two Gods. If (faith

label: text

Being Equal, they would be Two Invisibles, and consequently Two Gods. But Now, whilst the Son obeys his Father in all things; though He himself also be God, yet by his Obedience he declares his Father to be The One God, from whom also he derives his Original: And therefore he could not make

label: header

content: make Two Gods, because he did not make Two original Principles. [Here come in the corrupt Words cited by your Friend.] For all things being made subject to him as Son, by his Father; be himself, together with all things under him, being subject to his Father, is proved to be the Son indeed of the Father, but of all other things the Lord and God. The Son indeed is shown to be God, because Divinity is communicated and derived to him; and yet the Father is nevertheless proved to be The One God, whilst That Ma-

label: text
content: jesty and Divinity, which the Father communicates to the Son, is by the Son in acknowledgment continually returned back to the Father who gave it. So that God the Father, is justly stiled The God over All; and the Original even of the Son himself, whom he begat Lord of All: And at the same time the Son is the God of all Other things, because God the Father made all things subject to Him whom he begat. Thus Jesus Christ the Mediatour between God and Men, having from his Father All Creatures subjected to him as their God; himself with the

label: text

Ut merito Deus Pater, Omnium Deus sit, & Principium ipsius quoq; Filii fui quem Dominum genuit; Filius autem, ceterorum omnium Deus sit, quoniam omnibus illum Deus Pater praposuit quem genuit. Ità Mediator Dei & hominum Christus Jesus, omnis creature subjectam fibi habens a Patre proprio potestatem, qua Deus est; cum totà creatura subdita fibi, concors Patri suo Deo inventus, Unum & Solum & Verum DEVM Patrem suum breviter approbavit. cap. 31.

Wherefore both before and after his taking upon him human Flesh, and also after his Resurrection, he always did and does pay all Obedience to his Father. From

label: text
content: Your learned Friend understands these Texts, of an Unity of Nature; But what he means By Unity of Nature, he declares not. Most usually, what he says about it, amounts to an Unity of Person: As when he says, Hebovah our God, Hebovah is One; Which, in the Scripture, is expressly spoken of One Person; as has been shown above, No 1. So likewise, when he says

label: text
content: pag. 66. The Father and Son IS the One True God : and that Of him are all things, as HE is

label: text
content: Father; Through him, as HE is Son; and To him, as HE is the Holy Ghost; This is undeniably reducing them to One Person only. Nor does he any where show, what he means by That Unity of Nature; in which, Two Persons, Two Intelligent Agents, Equally Supreme, shall not be TWO Gods, that is, Two absolutely Supreme Governours. However, without knowing distinctly what he intends by Unity of Nature, he proceeds to prove that these Two Texts are meant

label: text
content: of an Unity of Nature : Not by considering the Context, and the Connexion of the words ; but by Two foreign Arguments. The first, is ; that the Name of God, [Jehovah,] is in several places of Scripture given to the Son: And in what manner This is done, I have just now explained, in the fore-going No 24. The second Argument is, a Collection of Sentences out of the Fathers: Some of which, do not at all mean what your Friend thinks of; (especially those of Novatian; As the Reader will find by comparing the Passages themselves with what immediately goes before and follows after, and with the other Passages which I have above cited out of the same Author :) And the Rest are no Proofs at all, what is the True Meaning of the Texts now before us.

label: text
content: That there is a reasonable Sense, in which the Father and the Son, though One be Self-existent and the Other not, may yet truly be affirmed to be of the same Nature, (though the Scripture never enters into such metaphysical Speculations,) I deny not. But the Question Now is, not what may or may not Truly be affirmed in general, but what is the True Meaning of the particular Texts at present before us. And This is to be gathered, not from our own or other Mens preconceived Hypotheses, but from the Scope and Connexion

label: text
content: Ver. 24, The Jews ask our Saviour, How long doft thou make us to doubt? If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly. Our Saviour replies, ver. 25, The works that I do in my Fathers Name, they bear witness of Me; That is, The Miracles which he worked by the Power and Authority of the Father, proved him to be in reality, what he pretended to be, the Messiah, sent forth from God.

label: text
content: Ver. 26, But ye (faith he) believe not because ye are not of my Sheep; That is they were prejudiced, vitious, and unreclaimable Perfons.

label: text

label: text
content: Ver. 29 O 30, For My Father, which Gave them me, is Greater than All; and none is able to pluck them out of my Father's hands : and I and my Father are One. That is : Since None can pluck them out of the Father's hands, and the Father has communicated His Power to the Son; therefore None can pluck them out of the Son's hands: So that, being in the Father's hands, or being in the Son's hands, is One and the

label: paragraph_title

label: text
content: same thing. [This is the natural Sense of the words, to which the Construction and Connexion of the whole Discourse leads us. And since the same words are used also in other places of Scripture in the very same Sense; As, Job. 17, 22, That They (my Disciples) may be One, even as We (I and the Father) are One; I in Them, and Thou in Me, that they may be made perfect in One; And 1 Cor. 3, 8, He that planteth, and he that watereth, (Paul and Apollos,) are One; 'Tis evident that the Sense, in which your Friend desires to take This Text, cannot be gathered from the Words themselves, nor from the Connexion of our Lord's Discourse, but must be proved (if it be proved at all,) by some other ways.]

label: text
content: Ver. 31 & 33. Upon this, the Jews took up Stones to stone him,—saying; we stone thee—for Blasphemy, and because that Thou, being a Man, makes thy self God. Meaning to accuse him, (as I have shown above, $ N^{o}23, $ ) not of affirming himself to be the Supreme, Self-existent Deity; nay, nor so much as of taking upon himself to be a Divine Person at all; but only of assuming to himself the Power and Authority of God. For, their Accusation, thou makes thy self God, was not founded (as your Friend imagines, pag. 70,) upon his affirming himself to be One with the Father,

label: paragraph_title
content: A Commentary

label: text
content: ther, (which Phrase it does not appear they thought at all difficult to be understood;) but the Accusation was founded upon his stiling God his Father, [ver. 25, 29 and 30,] and consequently making himself the Son of God. This appears plainly, from the Answer our Lord gave them in the words immediately following, ver. 34, 35, 36, Is it not written in your Law, I said, ye [Rulers and Magistrates] are Gods, [and Children of the most High?] If he called Them Gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken; Say ye of Him whom the Father bath sanctified and sent into the World, Thou blasphemeest, because I said, I AM THE SON OF GOD? From these words 'tis evident, that their Charge against him of Blasphemy, for which they went about to Stone him, was founded upon his calling God his Father, (see above, in No. 23,) or declaring himself to be the Son of God; which they, in their Anger, represented, by way of Aggravation, as making himself God.

label: text
content: Now in order to understand clearly what their Notion was of That Blasphemy, wherewith they charged him for calling himself the Son of God; it will be necessary to consider the parallel places, wherein the like Accusation is brought against him. Mark 2, 7; Upon his saying to a sick Man; Thy

label: header
content: on John 10; 30, 33.

label: text
content:
Thy Sins be forgiven thee; they answer, Why doth this Man thus speak Blasphemies? Who can forgive Sins, but God only? The Blasphemy they accuse him of here, was his taking upon himself, not the Person, but the Power and Authority of God, to forgive Sins. Again; when he was brought before Pilate, the Accusation against him was, Job. 19, 7, We have a Law, and by our Law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God. What they understood here by his making himself the Son of God, and thereby being guilty of Blasphemy; appears from the Account given in the other Three Gospels, of his Examination before the High-Priest in the Council. St Matt. 26, 63, Tell us (said the High-Priest) whether thou be the Christ the Son of God: Jesus faith unto him, Thou hast said: [ἐν λέγειω] not, Nevertheless; but, Moreover] I say unto you, Hereafter shall ye see the Son of Man sitting on the right-hand of Power, and coming in the Clouds of Heaven: Then the High-Priest rent his Clothes, saying, He bath spoken Blasphemy,——ye have heard his Blasphemy. St Mark relates it thus; ch. 14, 61, Art thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? And Jesus said, I am; And ye shall see the Son of Man sitting on the right-hand. &c. St Luke thus; ch. 22, 67, They asked him, saying, Art thou the Christ? He answered,

content: Hereafter shall the Son of Man sit on the right-hand of the Power of God: Then said they all, Art thou Then the Son of God? And he said unto them, ye say that I am. From these places compared together, it is evident, that That which they meant by asking him whether he was the Son of God, was to charge him with taking upon himself to be That Son of Man, of whom Daniel had prophesied, ch. 7, 13, I saw in the Night-visions, and behold, one like The Son of Man, came with the Clouds of Heaven, and came to the Antient of days, [to God the Father,] and they brought him near before him; And there was given him Dominion and Glory and a Kingdom, that all People, Nations, and Languages should serve him; His Dominion is an everlasting Dominion, which shall not pass away; and his Kingdom, that which shall not be destroyed. Our Lord's declaring Himself to be This Son of Man, the Christ, the Son of God, prophecied of by Daniel; was the Blasphemy, whereof the Jews accused him. And therefore 'tis probable, when they said they had a Law by which he ought to die, Joh. 19, 7; they did not mean That Law referred to in the Margin of our Bibles, Levit. 24; 15, 16; which threatens Death to him that curseth God, or blasphemeth the Name of the Lord; but rather That Law, Dent. 18, 20, which threatens

label: paragraph_title

label: text
content: threatens Death to Him that shall presume to speak a word in the Name of God, without being really sent by him. And accordingly, to This very same charge of Blasphemy. (in the place at present under our consideration, John 10, 33.) we find our Saviour replying, (not what your Learned Friend would have expected in His Hypothesis, but) that he was really sent from the Father, spake in his Name, worked by his Power, and was no Deceiver: Ver. 32, Many good Works have I showed you from my Father. Ver. 36, Say ye of Him whom the Father hath sanctified and sent into the World, Thou Blasphemest, because I said, I am the Son of God? And ver. 37, 38, If I do not the Works of my Father, [if my Works are not really such, as prove me to be sent of Cod, and to act by his Power,] believe me not: But if I do, though ye believe not Me, believe the Works; that ye may know and believe, that the Father is in Me, and I in Him.

And the Meaning of Both is fully explained, as by the Whole Scope of our Saviour's Discourse in this place, so by those other parallel Expressions, ch. 6, 56, He that eateth my Flesh and drinketh my Blood, dwelleth in Me, and K4 I in

label: text
content: I conclude This Head with a Passage out of Tertullian; who, though a Montanist, and One, who in this very Book against Praxeas affords your Friend more Citations to his Purpose, than are to be found in all the other Writers of the Three First Centuries put together, yet Thus commenteth

label: text
content: the Text we are Now upon. Concerning his Sheep also our Lord says, that none could take them out of his hand. For my Father, who gave them me, is Greater than All; and I and the Father are One. One Thing, he says; not One Person. For, One Thing, in the neuter Gender, does not express Identity, but Union, Likeness, Conjunction, the Love of the Father towards the Son, and the Obedience of the Son to the Will of his Father. When he says, I and the Father are One; he shows that they are Two Persons, whom he so joys equally together. For the same reason,

label: text
content: De ovibus etiam suis, quod nemo illas de manu ejus eriperet. Pater enim quod mihi dedit, majus est omnibus ; &, Ego for Pater Unum sumus. — Unum sumus, non, Unus sumus. — Unum dicit, neutrali verbo; qued non pertinet ad Singularitatem, sed ad Unitatem, ad Similitudinem, ad Conjunctionem; ad Dilectionem Patris, qui Filium diligit; & ad obsequium Filii, qui voluntati Patris obsequitur. Unum sumus, dicens, Ego for Pater; ostendit duos esse, quos aquat & jungit. Adeo addit etiam mulra se opera a Patre ostendisse, quorum nihil lapidari mereretur. Et ne putarent ideo se illum lapidare debere, quasi se Deum ipsum, id est Patrem, voluisset intelligi; quia djxerat, Ego for Pater Unum sumus; qua Filium Dei Deum ostendens, non qua iplum Deum : Si in lege, inquit, scriptum est, Ego dixi, vos diii estis; & non potest be.

label: text
content: solvi Scriptura; quem Pater sanctificavit, & misit in mundum, vos eum blasphemare dicitis, quia dixi, Filius Dei sum? Si non facio opera Patris mei, nolite credere; si vero facio, & Mihi credere non vultis, vel propter opera credite: Et scirote qudd ego in Patre sim, & Pater in Me. Per opera ergo erat pater in filio, & filius in Patre; & ita per opera intelligimus Unum esse Patrem & Filium. Adeo totum hoc perseverabat inducere, ut duo tamen crederentur in una virtute; quia aliter Filius credi non posset, nifi duo crederentur. Adverf.Praxeam. c. 22.

content: be adds also that he had shown them many Works from the Father, for none of which be deserved to be Stoned. And least they should think he deserved to be Stoned, as making himself to be God Himself, that is, the Father; by saying, that He and the Father were One; (by which he meant that He was God as being The Son of God, not as being GOD HIMSELF;) he therefore adds further, saying; If it is

label: text
content: written in the Law, I said ye are Gods, and the Scripture cannot be broken; say ye of Him whom the Father hath sanctified and sent into the World, Thou blasphemeest, because I said I am the Son of God? If I do not the Works of my Father, believe me not : But if I do, and ye believe not Me, believe me for the very Works sake: And know, that I am in the Father, and the Father in Me. By the Works therefore was the Father in the Son, and the Son in the Father; and so we understand the Father and the Son to be One, by the Works. Thus the whole of our Lords Discourse leads us to believe, that though they are One in Power, they are nevertheless Two Persons: Because otherwise it could not

label: text
content: Thus also Novatian: If Christ (faith he) had been the Father, as the Hereticks imagine; he would have said, I and my Father Am One, [Unus, One Person.] But One, in the Neuter Gender, [Unum, One Thing,] signifies Agreement of Fellowship, not Unity of Person. So that the Father and Son are One Thing, by Agreement and Love. The Apostle Paul also takes notice of this Unity of

label: text
content: Agreement, with a Difference of Persons. He that planteth, faith be, and he that watereth, are One, [One Thing.] Now every body knows, that yet Apollos was One Man, and Paul another, and not Paul and Apollos One and the Same Man.

label: text
content: When Isaiah in his Vifion saw the Glory of God, he foresaw the Glory wherein Christ was to be revealed: And the Glory it self which he Then saw, being the Visible Image of the Invisible God, was (in the unanimous Opinion of All the Ancient Fathers) the Son representing the Person of the Invisible Father. See my Scripture-doctrine, Part I. No 597, 616.

label: text
content: Against This, (which is very plain and intelligible, as well as the constant Doctrine of the Ancients,) your learned Friend alleges neither Arguments of Reason, nor the Authority of Antiquity. He adds only a remote and very obscure Discourse, concerning Christ's having a Name and Power and Glory of his own, as well as his Fathers; which is very true, but not to the purpose: Concerning a personal, but not real, difference of Glory; which is a Distinction very dark and obscure: Concerning a Name derived from the Father with the Person of the Son, referred to in the Form of Baptism; as if, being baptised into the Name of Christ, was not being baptised into the Profession of his Religion, but into the Name itself taken (as they speak) technically, materially, or cabbalistically: Concerning an Unity of Essence inferred from an Unity of Essential Glory, and an Unity of Glory from an Unity of Essence; which

label: header

label: text
content: which is a part of Metaphysicks very hard to be understood, and which the Scripture never meddles with: Lastly, concerning Two Persons represented by One Glory or Appearance, (which yet is not the Cafe, but, on the contrary, One Person's being the Glory or Representation of Another, the Visible representing the Invisible;) which, he says, 'tis natural to conclude is with this Design, that we should believe the Two Persons to be One Being; Which, I think, is a manifest Contradiction in Terms.

label: text
content: And here therefore at length your Friend joyns issue with me. The most remarkable thing (he says) in the Learned Doctor's Note upon the Text, and which I take to be the Key of his whole Book, is his confounding Individual Being and Person, as if they were Terms of the same Import; and then ranking those among the Followers of Sabellius, who hold the Father and Son to be One and the same Individual Being. Well then: If a Person be not an Intelligent Agent, and an Intelligent Agent an $ ^{*} $ Individual Intelligent Being, (which is the common and natural Notion

(says the learned Bishop Bull.) is, in things induced with Understanding, the same as Person. Defenf. Self. 2, cap. 9, §. 11. See also a large Passage of Justin

Will he tell us what Such a Person is, which is no Being; or how Modes of Substistence, mere abstract Notions, can be Intelligent Agents, without having so much as any real Existence at all? Or, of what Benefit can it possibly be, to make Use of words which have no Signification? Your Friend cannot here reply, that these things are a Mystery. For we are not now speaking about the

label: footnote
content: Justin Martyr in the latter part of his Dialogue with Trypho; where, speaking against those, who taught that the Son [ἀτμιστον χὰ ἄχωεισον τῶ πάτερος τυπιν τὴν δυναμνὸν πελεχεν. οὐπερ τεγπον τοῦ ἡλιὴ φασι φώς εἰπὸ γὰς είναι ἀτμιστον χὰ ἄχωεisinον σύνταῖν συναφοφεηται τοῦ φώς] was only a Power emitted from the Father, so as not to be really distinct from him, in like manner as Men say the Light of the Sun is upon Earth, yet so as not to be a real Distinct thing from the Sun in the Heavens, but, when the Sun sets, the Light also goes away with it; he, on the contrary, explains his Own Opinion to be, that as Angels are permanent Beings, and not mere Powers, so the Son, whom the Scripture calls [Θεοὺν χὰ Αγγελον] both God and an Angel, [ὃχώς τοῦ ἡλιὴ φασι φώσμα μόνου αειμίται, αλλά η αειμίτω έπειν πέσαι,] is not, like the Light of the Sun, a mere Name (or Power,] but a really distinct Being, begotten from the Father by his Power and Will; not by Division, as if the Father's Substance could be parted, as all corporeal things are divided and parted, and thereby become different from what they were before Part was taken from them; but as One Fire is lighted from another, [so as to be really distinct from it,] and yet the former suffers thereby no Diminution.

label: text
content: We must then be content to hear what your Friend, without having any distinct Notion of his own, what a Person is; has to object against My Notion of it, which is the common and natural Notion of All Mankind who never learnt the Jargon of the Schools. Why; "if God (faith be) be [οἱ ωὴν] Being, and God be individually One, and Being individually One; and the Son, no less than the Father, be True God, as has been already proved; then must the Father and the Son be One and the same Individual Being, that is, there must be Two Persons in One and the same Individual Being". The Conclusion, [Two Persons in One and the same Individual Uncompounded Being,] is an express Contradiction; and therefore the Premises must of necessity be Faulty somewhere. And indeed the Fault is very evident. God is not only [οἱ ωὴν] individually One Being, but also [οἱ ωὴν] individually One Intelligent Agent or Person, as has been shown above, No 1. And therefore if the Son's being True God, proves him

him to be o' œv, it will prove him to be, not only the same individual Being, but also the same individual Person with the Father. Which is more than your Friend intended to infer. And therefore the Son's being True God, must not be understood to signify that he is o' œv, but that He has True Divinity (which False Gods have not,) communicated to him from Him who is Alone o' œv. But your Friend proceeds:

"Since (faith be) the One True God is but One individual Being; and the Father is This One True God; the Son, if he is a distinct individual Being from the Father, must be distinct from the One True God, that is, be no True God himself at all; Which is contrary to 1 John. 5, 20". Thus Gen. 16, 10, The ANGEL of the Lord said unto her, I will multiply thy Seed exceedingly. Again, Gen. 31; 11, 13, The ANGEL of God spake unto me in a Dream, saying,——I am the GOD of Bethel, where——thou vowedst a Vow unto me. label: text
content: What your Friend alleges upon this Head; viz. that Christ is not excluded from being the God of the Patriarchs, (pag. 76;) that Christ is the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, (pag. 76;) that Christ is the Person who spake to Moses, and called himself the God of the Patriarchs, (pag. 77;) that Christ is stiled Hebovah, in distinction from the Person of the Father, [which yet may be controverted,] Gen. 19, 24, (pag. 78;) All This is in no wise contrary to any thing I have asserted. But then the Inference he draws, viz. that therefore the Son with the Father is the Necessary Being it self; This, as it is an express Contradiction, so it is also directly contrary both to the Text, and to the Opinion of all the Antient Fathers: See my Scripture-doctrine, Part I, No. 597 & 616. label: text
content: Of the Two Arguments your Learned Friend alleges for understanding these words concerning the Person of Christ, the first is the Context or Connexion of the words. The Apostle in the preceding Verse, encourages Christians to imitate their own Pastors in the Constancy of their Faith; the Object of which was Jesus Christ, who was no Person of a modern Date, but the same Yesterday, and to day, and for ever. Thus your Learned Friend. But Where now is the Force of This Argument? Imitate your own Pastors, because the Person of Christ is always the same. The Context, I think, plainly shows the other to be the True Sense: Adhere to the Faith of the Apostles who first instructed you, and be not carried about with divers new Doctrines; For the Doctrine of Christ is always One and the same,

Your Learned Friend joins these two Notions together; making that which is literal, to be at the same time figurative; and that which is only figurative, to be at the same time literal also: Which is a manifest Confusion and Impossibility. The latter of the Two Notions I now mentioned, is (I think) the more agreeable to the New Testament.

content: Testament. The Son of God is That Divine Person, by whom the Wisdom of the Father is manifested, and his Will revealed to all his Creatures; And upon That Account (as I observed,) His Name (says the Scripture) is called The WORD of God, ἀγλείτην ὑνομας ἄπτῶν, ὁ λόγος τὸ θεῶν, Rev. 19, 13. And if the Gospel of St John was written after the Revelation, (as is not improbable;) then the Reason of Christ's being called The Word, or That Word, in the first Verse of that Gospel, is the same with regard to this passage in the Revelation; as his being so frequently stiled in the Gospels, The Son of Man, or That Son of Man, is with regard to the person so stiled and described in the prophecy of Daniel, ch. 7, 13. Now because the word [λόγος] happens also to signify, Reason; hence the Authors your Friend cites, conclude, that Christ is literally the Reason or Wisdom of the Father; and, by Consequence, no Person at all. There are several other Passages in the New Testament, wherein Christ is called likewise the Power and the Righteousness of God: Very elegantly and emphatically; because by Him is manifested the Power, and by him is set forth in a most conspicuous manner The Righteousness [διαγγοσυν, πρυχ, The Mercy] of the Father. From hence the same Authors might have argued.

And by the same Argument that they infer in the other case, that the Father considered distinctly without the Son, would be [αλο-γεὺς ἐπὶ αφθ] a Being void of Reason and Wisdom; by the same Argument they might here likewise have inferred, that the Father considered distinctly without the Son, would be a Being void of Power and void of Mercy. content: The Meaning of This Text, I said, seemed to Me to be This: Esaias, by the Revelation of the Holy Ghost, saw God sitting upon the Throne of his Glory, and heard him saying Go &c. Esai. 6; 1, 9. Thus St John in the Apocalypse, being in the Spirit, (Rev. 1, 10,) saw God sitting upon his Throne, and beheld Christ in his Glory. And the words which Christ himself spake, (Rev. ch. 2, & ch. 3,) are in the very same Chapters said to be what the Spirit faith unto the Churches. So here likewise, what Esaias in the Spirit heard God speaking, is said to be spoken by the Holy Ghost. Whatever God speaks, may very properly be said to be spoken by the Holy Ghost, because God always speaks to his Prophets by the Inspiration of his Holy Spirit: And whatever is spoken by the Holy Ghost, may no less properly be said to be spoken by God, because 'tis spoken to the Prophets by That Spirit which God has

label: text
content: on Acts 28: 25, 26, 27. has given them. In the Revelation, ch. II, ver. I, 3, even an inferiour Angel is introduced as speaking in the Perfon of God : The Angel stood, saying ; I will give Power unto MY two Witnesses, &c.

label: text
content: Your learned Friend fairly acknowledges, that the Glory which appeared to Isaiah, ch. 6, is the Glory of the Father; even the same which appeared to St John, Rev. 4; 2, 8. But the same Glory (he says) is also called the Glory of the Son, Joh. 12, 41: How That Text is to be understood, I have shown above, in my Note upon the place, No 27. And the same Glory, (your Friend goes on,) is, in the place now before us, said to be the Glory of the Holy Ghost: That's very wonderful; for there is not one Syllable about Glory, either in the Text or Context. But he adds his reason for what he affirms; For the Glory or Lord, (faith be,) which spake to the Prophet, is called here the Holy Ghost: But That cannot be; because neither in the Old Testament nor in the New, is the Holy Ghost at any time stiled Lord; but, on the contrary, the Prophets are always represented as seeing those Visions by the Inspiration of the Holy Ghost, in which Visions they hear God or the Lord speaking. However, from hence your Friend collects with great Probability, (so he expresses himself,

label: paragraph_title
content: A Commentary

label: text
content: himself, much more modestly than many Writers,) the Unity or Identity of Nature of the Three Persons. But the Confusion that appears in This Expression, shows there is not That Clearness there should be in his Notion. For though between Two Individuals there may be an UNITY of Nature, as Two Men are (ομοθισιοι) of the same Common humane Nature; yet Two Individuals cannot, without an express Contradiction, have an IDENTITY of Nature; as Two Persons cannot be (ταυπτεσοι or μονθεσιιοι) of the same Individual or Identical Nature, because Then One of those Two Persons would be the same Person which the Other of them is.

label: text
content: The Passages he cites out of the Jewish Rabbies, (if they prove any thing,) prove either that those Rabbies took the Holy Ghost to be only another Title for God the Father himself, or else that they understood him to be a Person speaking in the Name of God the Father. And if there be any places in the Scripture itself, wherein the Spirit of God seems to be put figuratively for God himself, in like manner as the Spirit of a Man signifies the Man himself; yet such places do not at all favour your Friend's Hypothesis, but much rather the Sabellian or Socinian Notion; 'till, by being compared with other parallel places, their True Meaning

label: text
content: The Texts in the second and third Chapters of the Revelation, where the words of Christ are said to be what the Spirit faith unto the Churches, are thus explained by your Friend: Because (faith he) the One Glory of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, was manifested in the Humane Nature of Christ, though the Word only was personally united to it; are the words of Christ attributed to the Spirit. To Me, the Reason of This Expression [what the SPIRIT faith unto the Churches,] seems rather to be This; that 'twas by being in the Spirit, (ch. 1, 10,) 'twas by the Inspiration of the Spirit, that St John saw That Vision, wherein Christ was represented as speaking to him those words. Which of these two Interpretations is the more reasonable and intelligible, must be left to the Reader to judge.
