label: text
content: MATT. XII, 31. The Blasphemy against the Holy Ghost, shall not be forgiven unto Men : c.

label: text
content: By the Holy Ghost here, was meant (I said) not the Person, but the Works of the Holy Ghost : For no reason can be given, why Blaasphemy against the Person of the Spirit of God, should be more unpardonable, than Blaasphemy against the Person of the Son of God, or than Blaasphemy against the Person of God [the Father] himself. But the Works of the Spirit, being the greatest and last Means of Conviction that God ever intended to afford Men ; the rejecting of Them, was consequently the Highest Aggravation of Guilt.

label: text
content: To this, your Friend replies : Where This Doctrine, [that Blasphemy against God the Father, and the Son of God, are pardonable,]

label: aside_text
content:
In the Scripture doctrine, N° 1121.
In the Answer, pag. 125.

label: paragraph_title

label: text
content: ble,] is to be found, is hard to tell; The Text does not seem to infer it, nor the parallel places in the rest of the Evangelists. I answer: 'Tis to be found in the Words immediately going before the Text: ALL manner of Sin and BLASPHEMY shall be forgiven unto Men; [In St Mark it is, All Sins shall be forgiven unto the Sons of Men, and Blasphemies wherewith soever they shall blaspheme:] But the Blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven unto Men.

label: text
content: But he proceeds: Blasphemy against the Father (he says) is unpardonable, according to Levit. XXIV, 16, He that blasphemeth the Name of the Lord, shall surely be put to Death. I answer: A Capital Crime, is one thing; and what our Saviour says shall never be forgiven, is another.

label: text
content: Your Friend replies : The Jewish Doctors were of another Mind : They had a Tradition among them, that there were certain Crimes, that excluded the Sinners from having Any Portion in the World to come : Among which, was pronouncing the Name Jehovah according to its Letters : Now they looked upon the Egyptian to have cursed God, by such a Prominciation of the Sacred Name : The Consequence of which is, that his Blasphemy was irremissible in the World to come. But this their Reasoning was grounded up-

label: header
content: on Matt. 12, 31.

label: text
content: on so weak a Superstition, that he does not think fit to insist much upon it.

label: text
content: He goes on therefore to another Argument : If Any Crime is unpardonable, Blasphemy doubtless against the God of Heaven, or the Person of the Father, is so ; as being an Act of open Defiance and most provoking Insolence. I answer : Though no Crime is, in its own Nature, greater than Blasphemy against God ; yet a Crime may, upon account of certain Circumstances, become more unpardonable, as being more remote from Repentance. Of This Kind is Blaspheming the Greatest and Last Means of Conviction ; ascribing the most beneficial , as well as most powerful Works, to an unclean Spirit ; and thereby taking away all possible means of distinguishing Good from Evil : Which therefore our Saviour does accordingly in express Words here declare to be more unpardonable than Any other Blasphemy whatsoever.

label: text
content: The Texts he alleges out of the Epistle to the Hebrews, and out of St John, are by almost All Divines understood, not of a Sin absolutely unpardonable, but of a Sin exceedingly difficult to be amended and pardoned; namely Total Apostacy from Christianity. And if it was indeed absolutely unpardonable, yet it would be upon the same Account as the Sin in the Text is declared to be so; namely, because it is blasphemously renouncing the last Means of Conviction and Amendment. label: text
content: 2 COR. III. 17, 18. The Lord is That Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is Liberty.

label: text
content: But we All with open Face, beholding as in a Glass the Glory of the Lord, are changed into the same Image from Glory to Glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.

label: text
content: For the clearer Understanding the True Meaning of these Words, it will be proper to consider the whole Scope of the Apostles Discourse in this Chapter. The Holy Ghost having been poured forth upon the Apostles at Pentecost in so very singular and plentiful a manner, as that, before that time, it is said comparatively, not to have been given at all, Joh. 7, 39; hence Paul in the 8th Verse of this Chapter, elegantly stiles the Gospel, by way of Eminence, The Ministration of the Spirit. And from That Consideration, through the Whole Chapter, magnifies the Doctrine of Christ, as being more clear and plain, more powerful and efficacious, more illustrious and glorious, than the Law of Moses. Ver. 3. Te are (faith he) the Epifle of Christ, ministred by Us, written not with Ink, but with the

label: text
content:
the Spirit of the Living God; not in Tables of Stone, but in fleshy Tables of the Heart: That is; The Power and Efficacy of the Gospel, is as much greater than that of the Law, as can be expresst by comparing that which is written in a Book, with that which is imprinted inwardly in the very Heart and Soul itself. The same Argument he pursues, ver. 6, God hath made us able Ministers of the New Testament, not of the Letter, but of the Spirit; for the Letter killeth, but the Spirit giveth Life: That is; The Gospel gives us those Spiritual Precepts, whereof the Legal Ordinances were but Types and Shadows; and teaches us the way to eternal Life, whereas the Rigour of the Law could end only in Mens condemnation. And from hence he proceeds to magnify the glorious Manifestation of the Gospel, by comparing it with the Glory that shined in Moses's Countenance; which, though so bright that the Children of Israel could not stedfastly behold it, yet was but temporary and transient, and only a Type or Figure of That permanent Glory of the Gospel, which was to continue for ever: Ver. 7. If the Ministration of Death, written and engraven in Stones, was glorious, so that the Children of Israel could not stedfastly behold the Face of Moses, for the Glory of his Countenance, which Glory was to be done away; How shall not the Ministration of the

N Spirit

label: paragraph_title
content: A Commentary

label: text
content: Spirit be rather glorious For if the Ministration of Condemnation be Glory, much more doth the Ministration of Righteousness, (of Fussification, it should be rendred,) exceed in Glory:——For if That which was done away was glorious, much more That which remaineth (that which is Perpetual) is glorious. And hereupon he takes occasion elegantly to describe the Blindness of the Jews after our Saviour's time, in not seeing through the Types and Figures of the Old Testament; by comparing it to the Veil which Moses put upon his Face to conceal the Brightness of it: Ver. 14, 15, 16, Their Minds (faith he) were blinded; For until this day remaineth the same Veil untaken away, in the reading of the Old Testament; which Veil is done away in Christ: But even unto this day, when Moses is read, the Veil is upon their Heart: Nevertheless when it [when the Heart of the People of the Jews] shall turn to the Lord [shall be converted to Christ.] the Veil shall be taken away: As he had said just before, ver. 14, which Veil is done away in Christ.

label: text
content: And then he fums up all, and concludes his whole Discourse, in the Words of the Text now before us : Ver. 17 ;

label: text
content: Now the Lord is that Spirit.] The Lord; that is, Christ, in or by whom, in or by whose Gospel, (he had said, ver. 14,) the Veil is done away; and to whom, (he had said,

label: text
content: faid, ver. 16,) the Jews should be converted : This Lord, even Christ, is That Spirit which the Apostle had been speaking of through the Whole Chapter. His Meaning therefore is : The Gospel or Doctrine of Christ, is the Spirit, the End and Design of the Law, which giveth Life, or shows Men the way to Justification ; in opposition to the dead Letter and to the Rigour of the Law, which leads only to Condemnation. 'Tis that Spirit or final Intent of the Law, which is to continue for ever ; in opposition to those mere Types and Shadows, which were soon to be done away. 'Tis that Spirit or full Meaning and Signification of the Law, which is opposed to the Veil of Ignorance and partial Understanding of it.

label: text
content: [Chrift, or the Gospel of Christ, is here said to be the Spirit; after the same manner of speaking, as he is affirmed in other places of Scripture to be The Way, The Truth, The Life, The Wisdom or Power of God, Our Righteousness, and the like.]

label: text
content: And where the Spirit of the Lord is there is Liberty.] That is : Where this Ministration of the Spirit, (ver. 8;) this Manifestation of the Truth, (ver. 2, of the following Chapter,) prevails ; where the Gospel is received and embraced ; There is Liberty. Liberty, from the Bondage and Yoke of Ceremonies; Liberty, from the N 2 Domi-

label: paragraph_title
content: A Commentary

label: text
content: Dominion and Slavery of Sin ; Liberty, from the Rigour and Terrour of the Law, from the Ministration of Condemnation, ver. 9, from the Ministration of Death, ver. 7; But most immediately, Liberty from that Veil of Ignorance and Obscurity, which remained upon the Hearts, and perplexed the Understandings of the unbelieving Jews, when the Old Testament was read to them: In opposition to which, the Apostle argues, ver. 12, that WE use great plainness of Speech, and not as Moses which put a Veil over his Face.

label: text
content: But We All with open Face.] This is not said in opposition to what went before, but by way of Explication of, or Inference from, the Words immediately fore-going. It should not therefore have been rendred [BUT,] but [AND.] Where the Spirit of the Lord is, where the Gospel prevails, There is Liberty; AND We all, or, And Therefore we all, all true Christians, do with open Face, not through an obscure Veil, as did the Jews, behold the Glory of the Lord.

label: text
content: With open Face.] That is, clearly, plainly, and distinctly: Not in Types and Shadows, not in obscure Glimpses and feint Representations, not in remote Hints and distant Prospects; but with a full and direct View, an immediate Intuition, as of the Substance and reality, of things present and actually

label: text
content: actually before us. We behold the Mystery of God in Christ, not as the Children of Israel saw the Brightness of Moses's Countenance through the Veil, (which is what the Apostle here alludes to;) but with open Face, as Moses himself is described to have seen the Lord, when the Lord spake unto him Face to Face, as a Man speaketh unto his Friend, Exod. 33, 11.

label: text
content: Beholding the Glory of the Lord.] That is; the Clear and Glorious Manifestation of the Will of God by the Gospel. For so the Gospel is stiled, The Riches of Gods GLORY, Rom. 9, 23; the Riches of the GLORY of this Mystery, Col. 1, 27; the GLORY as of the only-begotten of the Father, full of Grace and Truth, Joh. 1, 14; the Light of the GLORIOUS Gospel of Christ, who is the Image of God, 2 Cor. 4, 4; And ver. 6, The Light of the Knowledge of the GLORY of God, shining in our Heart. The Words of that whole Verse, are very remarkable: God, who hath commanded the Light to shine out of Darkness, (that is, who manifested his Glory originally in the First Creation of Things,) hath shined in our Hearts, (that is, hath manifested his Glory the second time no less confpicuously in our Redemption,) to give the Light of the Knowledge of the GLORY of God, in the Face of Jesus Christ. And these two last Expressions; Christ's being the IMAGE of God;

label: paragraph_title
content: A Commentary

label: text
content: and the Light of the Knowledge of God's Glory shining upon us in the FACE (or in the Person) of Christ; open to us the Ground and Meaning of that Similitude, which the Apostle here interpoes;

label: text
content:
Beholding, as in a GLASS, the Glory of the Lord.] That which he hereby intended to express, is; that in Christ, who is the Image of the Invisible God, and the Great Revealer of his Will, we clearly and plainly behold the whole Pleasure of God towards us. For the Father, no Man hath seen at any time; no Man Hath seen, nor Can see; but the only-begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, He hath declared him; And hath declared him so plainly, that he who hath seen ME, faith our Saviour, has seen the FATHER, Joh. 14, 9.

There is a Phrase very like to this in the Text before us, used in a contrary Sense by the same Apostle, I Cor. 13, 12, Now we see through a GLASS darkly, but Then Face to Face. In which Passage; seeing THROUGH a GLASS, signifies seeing darkly or obscurely, in opposition to beholding plainly, Face to Face: But here, in the present Text, beholding as IN a GLASS, signifies on the contrary, seeing clearly or plainly; and is the very same as, beholding Face to Face. The Words in the Original, are in Both places more expressive, than in the Translation; and show plainly the Reason

label: text
content: of This different Signification. In One place, the Word, which we render, Glass, signifies a Perspective-glass, [βλέπομεν διεσπίλρει] which brings distant things into the Reach indeed of our Sight, but still very obscurely, imperfectly, and indistinctly; and does therefore very elegantly, and by a most proper Similitude, express That View of a Future State, which we have by Faith and not by Sight. But now in This Other place, the Word which we render, Glass, [κατοωιλειζόμενοι] signifies a Mirroir or Looking-glass, which on the contrary represents things plainly and distinctly, Face to Face; and therefore no less elegantly represents that clear Light of the Knowledge of the Glory and Will of God, which shines to us (faith the Apostle) in the FACE of Jesus Christ.

label: text
content: Are changed into the same Image.] That is: As Christ is, by Nature, the perfect Image of God; so We, by communication of Light and Knowledge from him, and by the Practise of Righteousness and true Holiness in Obedience to him and Imitation of him, are transformed into the same Image. As Christ is, by Nature, the Son of God; so We, by Adoption and by the Fruits of the Spirit dwelling in us, have This Love bestowed upon us, that We also should be called The Sons of God: For of his Fulness have we all received, and Grace for Grace, N 4 Joh.

label: text
content: Your learned Friend, contends for quite another Interpretation of this whole Text; and thinks that the word, Lord, in the 17th verse, signifies not Christ, but the Holy Ghost: So that when the Apostle says, The Lord is That Spirit, his Meaning will be, The Holy Ghost is that Spirit. The reasons he gives for this Interpretation, are very dark and obscure; and make the whole Text very intricate, by a strange Confusion of Persons. That the word, Lord, in that place, cannot possibly signify the Holy Ghost, is (I think) very evident from the following considerations.

label: text
content: 1. The whole Scope and Connexion of the Apostles Discourse from the beginning of the Chapter to the End, is very clear, natural and elegant, according to the Explication I have given of it above; taking the word, Lord, in the 17th verse, to signify Christ, according to the general style of the New Testament. Whereas, according to your Friends interpretation, the whole is made intricate and obscure, by a confused Transition from one person to another.

label: text
content: 2. The Context immediately going before and following, necessarily determines the

label: paragraph_title
content: A Commentary

label: text
content: the word, Lord, in the 17th verse, to signify Christ. For in the 14th verse, the Apostle had said, that the Veil of ignorance, which is upon the Heart of the unbelieving Jews when the old Testament is read, is done away in Christ, that is, is removed when by believing the Gospel they are instructed rightly to understand the typical expressions in the old Testament. In the 16th verse he repeats the same Sense again in these words, When it [the Heart of the People of the Jews] shall turn to the Lord, the Veil shall be taken away: To turn to the Lord, that the Veil may be taken away; evidently means, being converted to Christ, [or embracing the Gospel,] in or by whom, he had said just before, the Veil is done away; And therefore when he goes on, ver. 17, Now the Lord —; it is most manifest that the word, Lord, must mean that very same Lord, who is spoken of in the 16th verse, and who in the 14th verse is expressly called Christ. Wherefore 'tis very wonderful your learned Friend should affirm, (pag. 134,) that Nothing occurs in the whole Context to determine the word to this Sense; when the very words immediately fore-going, do by most necessary and evident construction so determine it. And as to the words next following; far from confirming your Friends Interpretation, as he supposes; they also evidently show it to be

label: text
content: be impossible to be true: For when the Apostle adds, Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is Liberty; if the word, Lord, in the fore-going words, had signified the Holy Ghost, then the Spirit of the Lord would here have been as much as if he had said, The Spirit of the Holy Ghost, or the Spirit of the Spirit itself; which is manifestly impossible.

label: text
content: 3. Lastly; Were there no other Argument, it would be sufficient to allege, that your Friends understanding the word, Lord, in this place, to mean the Holy Ghost; is entirely contrary to the whole Language of the inspired Writings, and tends to introduce the utmost confusion. For neither in the Old, nor in the New Testament, is there any one place, where the Holy Ghost is ever spoken of under the Title of Lord, but always distinctly under his own proper personal Denomination, the Spirit of the Lord, or the Spirit of God, or the Holy Spirit. There are only Two Places (and those your Friend seems not to have been aware of,) wherein Basil, contrary to all the Writers in the Ages before him, understands the word, Lord, to mean the Holy Ghost. content: ANSW. The Difference between Christianity and Paganism, is This. The Pagans acknowledged many FALSE (fictitious) Gods, and many FALSE (fictitious) Lords: On the contrary, Christians acknowledge only One TRUE God, and only One TRUE Lord or Mediatour. There are (faith St Paul) that are called, (that is, there were feigned by the Heathens,) Gods many, and Lords many; But to Us [Christians,] there is but One God, [viz.] the Father, Of whom

Now to say, that besides the One True God, there cannot be also One True Lord or Mediatour; is an Argument, not against my Scheme in particular; but 'tis the Argument which Deists use, (with what reason, I have elsewhere shown,) against Christianity in general. Or to say, that there is also indeed One True Lord or Mediatour, but that That One True Lord is the same Individual with the One True God; What is This, but to affirm in other words, that the One Lord, Jesus Christ, B T whom are all things, is the One God, the Father, O F whom are all things? Which is overturning the Apostles whole Argument, and introducing an absolute Confusion of Persons. Our One God, says the Apostle, is the Father: If then the One Lord, Jesus Christ, be That One God, whom the Apostle defines to be the Father, of whom are all things; is not this expressly affirming that the Son is the Father? Than which, nothing can be more hard to understand, or to reconcile with the whole Doctrine of Scripture.

label: text
content: But why must Three Divine Beings, of Necessity be conceived as Three Gods? One God, the Almighty Father; and One Lord, the Only-begotten Son of That Almighty Father; and One Holy Spirit of God, the Spirit of That Almighty Father; are in our Creed

label: text
content: Creed represented to us as Three distinct Agents: And yet they are no more Three Gods, than they are Three Almighty Fathers, which is (according to the Creed) the Definition of God. One God, to whom Mediation is made; and One Mediatour, making Intercession for us to That One God, (which is St Paul's manner of speaking;) are no more Two Gods; than an Advocate with the Father, and the Father with whom that Advocate is, (which is St John's manner of expressing the same thing;) are Two Fathers. One Spirit, One Lord, One God and Father of all, who is above all; are by the Apostle represented to us, as Three distinct Agents: And yet they can no more truly be said to be Three Gods, than Each of them singly, (or than All of them together;) can be truly said to be The God and Father of All, who is Above All; Which is the Apostles Definition of the One Supreme God. Three perfectly co-ordinate, and equally Supreme Persons or Agents, (whatever Distinctions, or whatever Unity of Nature be supposed between them,) must of Necessity be conceived to be Three Gods, that is, Three Supreme Independent Governors of the Universe; because the proper Notion of God in Scripture, and in natural Reason also, as to all moral and religious Regards, is his being absolutely ὑπαντοκράτωρ, Supreme Ruler over All,

label: paragraph_title
content: An Answer to the Author

label: text
content: and ὀσκατὴρ πάντων, (Eph. 4, 6.) the Father or Author of all things: But, This Character being preserved entire, no other Power whatsoever ascribed or communicated to other Agents or Persons, can justly cause us to conceive more Gods than One. How and in what Sense the Son, though he be not That One God and Father of All, who is above All, may yet truly and properly be stiled God; has been largely explained in the fore-going Papers.

label: text
content: But now on the other side, if the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, be conceived to be All but One Individual Being; it follows of Necessity, that the Son and Holy Spirit have no Being at all; Which is an insuperable Difficulty in This learned Authors Scheme. For if each of these Characters belong to One and the same Individual Being; and the Father Alone be (as is acknowledged) That Whole Being; it follows evidently that the Son and Holy Spirit, either are Themselves The Father, (which he is not willing to allow;) or else have no real Being, no Existence at all, but can only be Modes, Powers, Characters or different Denominations of That One Supreme, that One Simple and Uncompounded Being, which is the Father of All. The plain Consequence of which is, that our Mediatour and Redeemer is only a Mere Man, in whom God the Father manifested himself

label: paragraph_title
content: of Some Considerations &c.

label: text
content: himself after an extraordinary manner; and that the Holy Spirit is nothing but a mere Virtue or Operation of the Father. Which Notion, how much soever it may be defended, as an Hypothesis, by bare Reasen, (as may be seen in the Socinian Writers ;) yet I can by no means see how it is to be reconciled with what is taught in Scripture. Befides : Since this Learned Writer always supposes his own Scheme, to be the same with That which from the Time of the Fourth Century has been stiled Orthodox; it deserves to be remarked on the contrary, that by his plainly making the Son to be, not ὁμοθυσίς, but ταυπέσιος with the Father, that is, One and the same Individual Being; his Assertion in reality appears to be the same with That, which from before the days of Photinus to the Times of the Schoolmen, has by the Council of Nice, and all following Councils been condemned as Heterodox.

For which reason, the Antient Fathers both before and after the Council of Nice, do almost unanimously alert, that the Son was begotten of the Father, not by Necessity of Nature, but by the ineffable Power of his Will: As I have shown at large in my Scripture-Doctrine, Part II, §. 17. For, the Creator signifying (in Scripture-phrase) the Father of all things, who created all things by his Son; if now there cannot possibly be any thing between the Supreme Father of All things, and That System of Beings which we call The Creature; it will of Necessity follow, that the Son of God must be either the Supreme Father himself, or else a mere Creature. To avoid this consequence, he is forced to suppose (pag. 129,) that the Son is something more than a mere Name, and yet not a real distinct Being; that is to say, that he is something between a Being and not a Being: Which is an undeniable Contradiction. I cannot but wonder, so learned a Writer should complain of My Scheme, for being what, after the most diligent Perusal, he cannot fully comprehend; and at the same time set up One in opposition to it, which of Necessity terminates either in a manifest Contradiction, or else in a Doctrine which of all others has always been esteemed the most Heterodox.

content: pag. 15. OBf. 'Did the Ifraelites worship Mofes, because the Lord said unto him, I have made thee a God unto Pharaoh?

label: text
content: ANSW. Honour or Worship is always due in proportion to the Authority and Power, the Dominion and Dignity, of the Person to whom it is paid: And where there is no proportion between the Dominion or Dignity of Two Persons at any time compared together, there is also consequently no proportion between the Honours due to them. The Israelites honoured Moses, as being what he was, not as being what he was not: They honoured him, as a Servant, not as the Son, of God: as a Man authorized from God to lead the People, not as being himself a Divine Person. Christians likewise worship Christ, as being what he is, not as being what he is not: They worship him as being the Son of God, not as being God the Father himself: They worship him, according to his real Powers and Attributes, as being That Divine Person, who having been originally in the Form of God, voluntarily took upon himself the Form of a Servant, and was therefore highly exalted of God, and had a Name given him above every Name, that at the Name of Jesus every knee should bow, [every thing should be subject

In That very Passage it self, Rom. 1, 20, θεότns signifies nothing else but Divine Power or Dominion; not the Substance of God, which this learned Author seems erroneously to think the Word Godhead signifies. The Words are, ἡτε αὐτῶι δὲν τῆς δύναμης ἡ δείότης, his eternal Power and Divinity or Divine Dominion. So likewise therefore in That other Passage, Col. 2, 9, In him dwelleth all the Fulness of the Godhead; the meaning is, the Fulness of Divine Power, Dominion and Authority: In like manner, as Col. 1, 19, It pleased the Father, that in Him should all Fulness dwell; and Job. 14, 10, The Father that dwelleth in Me, he doth the Works; That is, not the Person, but the Divine Power, [ἡ θεότns] of the Father, dwelleth in Christ. Thus the Word [θεότns Divinity,] Always signifies; in the same manner as αὐθρωπότεns, and all other Words of the like Formation. And 'tis as great an Abuse of Language, to suppose [θεοτns] the Deity or Divinity, that is, the Dominion of God, to signifie the Substance of God; as it would be to understand [αὐθρωπότεns] Manhood, to signifie the Substance of Man. Further: 'Tis worth observing upon this occasion, that not only θεότητα, the Divinity, or Supreme Dominion, of God; but even This other Word itself, θεοὺς God, has in Scripture, and in all Books of Morality and Religion, a relative Signification; and not, as in metaphysical Books, an Absolute One. As is evident from the relative Terms, which in moral Writings may always be joined with it. For instance: In the same manner as we say, my Father, my King, and the like; so it is proper also to say, my God, the God of Israel, the God of the Universe, and the like: Which Words are expressive of Dominion and Government. But, in the metaphysical way, it cannot be said, My Infinite Substance, The Infinite Substance of Israel, or the like. Which plainly shows in what Sense the Word Godhead, always ought to be understood in Theological Matters.

Because every Person is a Being, but every Being is not a Person; therefore εἰς, which is of the more limited Signification, and expresses intelligent Being or Person only, can never possibly be extended to signify Being in general: But εἴν, which signifies Being in general, may also be used of such a Being, as is an intelligent Being, that is, a Person. Therefore πὸ γεννησέν and πὸ αγον might properly be used by St Matthew and St Luke, as well as οὐαγωγο and οὐγεννησείς; because the Subject mentioned, (besides that perhaps πὸ πασιδίου is referred to), was equally both a Holy Thing and a Holy Person. But εἴν, in this place of St John, cannot signify One Being; because the Subject spoken of, being an Intelligent Being, it would consequently have meant the same as εἰς One Person: Which confessedly not being our Saviours intention to affirm, it follows of Necessity that the words must be understood figuratively, in the manner that has been above explained at large, pag. 144, ἀνc.

label: text
content: ANSW. This (I think) is an express Contradiction: For between Being and not Being there can be no middle. Whatever is not a Being, is no Being; and whatever is no Being, can at most be only a Name or Denomination, a Mode, Quality, Relation, or the like; things which have no Existence but in Our Conceptions, distinct from the Existence of the Substance to which they belong. The Schoolmen have endeavoured to find out something intermediate between Being and not Being, by means of what they call an internal Production: And the Learned Bp. Bull himself is forced finally to have recourse to this unintelligible Term of Art, (Sect. 4, cap. 4,) in order to maintain an Explication of the Unity of God upon such a Foot, as can very hardly be reconciled with his own Discourse in the rest of that excellent Section concerning the

content: the Subordination of the Son. For a Subordination of one Person to another, necessarily supposes the two Persons to be distinct. But now the Notion of internal Production, can in reality mean nothing else but to destroy That Distinctness; and consequently ends in an unavoidable Contradiction. For if internal Production was meant only in opposition to being extrinsic to God; in That Sense 'tis manifest that internal Production belongs equally to All Beings whatsoever; because In Him All things have their Being: But if internal Production means such a Production, as gives the thing produced no distinct Existence of its own; (which is what the Schoolmen aim at;) then 'tis manifest it signifies a Production of Nothing, that is, No Production at all. See a remarkable passage of Justin Martyr upon this Head, cited above, pag. 157, 158. Neither can it here reasonably be alledged, that these Expressions are mysterious: For though, if God himself had been pleased to reveal any thing in such Words as we could not distinctly understand, it would indeed have been very reasonable to believe firmly that those words had a distinct Meaning, though we apprehended it not: yet when Men invent Words, whose Signification They themselves cannot distinctly explain; it is then, on the other side, no less reasonable

The Question is not about Duration, or any other metaphysical Qualities, but about Dominion and Authority; which Alone is That which makes God to be God, (in the moral or religious sense of the Word,) ο πάντωνκράτωρ, Supreme over all. For Dominion and Duty are Relatives between Him that Governs and them which are governed. Metaphysical and Absolute Qualities, may be Objects of Admiration; but relative Dominion only, is the Foundation of Duty. Space

label: text
content: Space is Eternal, but it is not therefore God. If Matter were Infinite and Eternal, still it would not at all be our God. And if any other Being had any other Attributes whatsoever, yet still if it had not Dominion over Us, Neither should We owe any Duty to It. 'Tis Dominion only, that makes God to be God to Us; and therefore the Scripture so frequently uses the word τωντοκραττωρ, Supreme over all, as equivalent to the Title, God. Now in the Notion of Dominion, 'tis very evident that original and derived are Distinctions which make a plain and necessary Difference. Which is all that I contend for.

label: text
content: And now, having given a distinct and (I hope) satisfactory Answer to all the Objections that have hitherto been urged against me: I take leave upon this occasion to declare once for all; that as I have upon mature and long Consideration, and with the utmost Sincerity, drawn up my Thoughts upon This Subject, and laid them before the Publick, with my Reafons for them, as clearly as I am able; so I willingly submit what I have written, to the judgment of every honest and impartial Reader, who is capable of examining things of this Nature,

label: paragraph_title
content: An Answer to the Author

label: text
content: ture. To whom, if what I have offered has Weight and Truth on its side, it will, I make no doubt, approve itself: If it has not, I am content it should find no better Reception than it deserves. I desire not, to impose my Opinion upon any Man; but only to prevail with Men to study the Scripture, and to make It their only Rule in matters of Revelation; and that inquisitive Persons would be pleased to Compare what has been or shall be objected against me, with what I have said either in Answer to, or in order to obviate, such Objections. It would be endless for me to repeat the same things again and again, as often as any one shall please to tell the World he differs from me, without offering any New Arguments for such his Opinion. Whenever either my own further Searches, or the learned Enquiries of Others, convince me that I am mistaken in my present Notions, I shall think my self obliged to own it to the World. In the mean time I hope I may without Offense desire, that if I am Silent hereafter, it may be interpreted as a Declaration, that I see no reason to change my Sentiments. I have no Concern, but for Truth; and from whatever hand it comes, shall readily receive it: But what is not Truth, or does not to me appear so, I cannot embrace. And This I shall for the
